It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

frontier.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
frontier.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

frontier.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
frontier.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

frontier.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
frontier.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.

frontier.title: GenTranslate: Large Language Models are Generative Multilingual Speech and Machine Translators
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have stepped forward the development of multilingual speech and machine translation by its reduced representation errors and incorporated external knowledge. However, both translation tasks typically utilize beam search decoding and top-1 hypothesis selection for inference. These techniques struggle to fully exploit the rich information in the diverse N-best hypotheses, making them less optimal for translation tasks that require a single, high-quality output sequence. In this paper, we propose a new generative paradigm for translation tasks, namely GenTranslate, which builds upon LLMs to generate better results from the diverse translation versions in N-best list. Leveraging the rich linguistic knowledge and strong reasoning abilities of LLMs, our new paradigm can integrate the diverse N-best candidates to generate a higher-quality translation result. Furthermore, to support LLM finetuning, we build and release a HypoTranslate dataset that contains over 592K hypotheses-translation pairs in 11 languages. Experiments on various speech and machine translation benchmarks (e.g., FLEURS, CoVoST-2, WMT) demonstrate that our GenTranslate significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art model.

frontier.title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
frontier.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.

frontier.title: Bridging Task Planning and Execution for Language-Conditioned Bimanual Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. Videos and additional material are available on the Project Webpage: https://advrhumanoids.github.io/bridging-planning-execution/.

frontier.title: Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory?
frontier.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information, and when to revise existing topics, and every summary it produces stays linked to the original interactions as evidence. The runtime validates updates and automatically derives temporal, relational, and recent-memory views from the organized content. At query time, the agent chooses what to search and read, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed. On LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of agents organizing and using their own persistent memory through ordinary documents. Code is available at: https://github.com/Qi202/SoMem.

frontier.title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
frontier.abstract: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

frontier.title: CRAFT-AI: Capability and Requirement Alignment for Flexible Manufacturing through Agentic AI
frontier.abstract: One of the fundamental needs for reaching resilient production infrastructure is flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing production requirements into implementable system configurations. This paper introduces \textbf{CRAFT-AI}, an agentic AI approach combining natural language (NL) requirement interpretation, Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-based capability descriptions, and reusable engineering knowledge from existing manufacturing configurations. A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach is demonstrated using a Factory I/O prototype with twelve reference scenes and five illustrative manufacturing tasks of varying complexity, providing an initial feasibility assessment of the proposed AAS-enabled, system-level generative engineering approach. For the four valid user task descriptions, proper requirements, correct references to the relevant engineering knowledge, correct components and lastly a valid Factory I/O scene are generated. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, the user is informed about which requirements of the scene generation lack domain knowledge and also which sensor is not compatible with the selected raw material by the user with link to the related documentation. After fixing the task description, the correct scene is seamlessly generated. \textbf{CRAFT-AI} highlights the importance of safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation model-driven solutions.

frontier.title: DeltaForge: A Post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts VLA for Multi-Domain Autonomous Driving
frontier.abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.

frontier.title: GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.

frontier.title: Graph-Based RL for Sequential Rendezvous Planning with Multiple Patrolling USVs
frontier.abstract: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.

frontier.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
frontier.abstract: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

frontier.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
frontier.abstract: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

frontier.title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer
frontier.abstract: Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems. With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1. Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory). Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN. In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.

frontier.title: MNN-Pocket-0.3B Technical Report
frontier.abstract: This technical report presents MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a compact 300M-parameter dense language model designed for efficient on-device deployment and supporting context lengths of up to 32K tokens. With an INT4 deployment footprint of only 173 MB and decoding throughput of up to 466 tokens/s on iPad Pro M5 (Metal), it can be seamlessly integrated into applications on edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is developed through the co-design of its architecture, data, training pipeline, and inference system. Hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning balance model capability with on-device memory and compute constraints. A four-stage pre-training pipeline covering approximately 4.1 trillion high-quality Chinese and English tokens equips the model with broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. This is followed by a three-stage post-training pipeline comprising instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and quantization-aware training. Finally, hardware-specific optimizations in the MNN inference engine enable fast, memory-efficient inference and long-context processing. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MNN-Pocket-0.3B achieves frontier-level performance among models of comparable size, with particularly strong results in Chinese and English knowledge and reasoning, mathematics, coding, and instruction following. It consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models and even surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks. We release MNN-Pocket-0.3B with open weights and ready-to-use MNN deployment packages. We hope it will provide a practical foundation for capable, responsive, and memory-efficient edge applications while advancing research and development in on-device language models.

frontier.title: SCALE: Small-Model-First Concept Abstraction with LLM-Guided Experience Internalization
frontier.abstract: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. Experiments across ten random seeds show that historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%, hierarchical concept knowledge increases difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.

frontier.title: Thermo-VLA: A Thermal-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model with Gated Residual Modulation for Robotic Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: https://j-x-chen.github.io/Thermo-VLA-web/

frontier.title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
frontier.abstract: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.

HINT-VLM: Humanoid Interactive Navigation over Rough Terrain with Embodiment-Grounded Vision-Language Model
frontier.abstract: Humanoid robots have achieved significant progress in locomotion and manipulation, enabling traversal over rough terrain and richer interaction with the environment, such as moving obstacles. However, most traditional navigation methods assume non-interactive environments and focus only on traversal. While Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches relax this assumption, prior efforts have largely focused on flat environments and reactive interaction, rather than predicting object movability and planning ahead. These limitations become critical in outdoor rough-terrain scenarios, where robots must jointly reason about terrain traversability and object movability. In this work, we address NAMO for humanoid robots in cluttered outdoor rough terrain by proposing a hybrid planning framework that combines semantic priors from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) with embodied robot interaction data through a Gaussian process (GP) residual model. The GP corrects the VLM-derived movability prior to produce embodiment-grounded probabilistic movability estimates, which are then incorporated into hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning. The proposed approach allows humanoids to jointly leverage locomotion and manipulation for efficient and safe navigation, representing the first solution to NAMO in rough terrain through predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.

Data Fragmentation as a Critical Bottleneck in Disaster Response Planning: The EVAC-AI Case Study for Flood Risk Assessment
frontier.abstract: Coastal flood risk in regions such as Hampton Roads, Virginia, is constrained not by a lack of data, but by the fragmentation of that data across agencies, formats, and update cadences. This fragmentation directly undermines risk assessment for response planning: when hazard, infrastructure, and vulnerability data remain siloed, compound risk cannot be assessed as a single picture, and response decisions are made against an incomplete view. Addressing it requires three capabilities: integrating heterogeneous sources into a consistent representation, optimizing decisions by reasoning across interconnected systems such as transportation and urban planning, and coordinating role-specific access to a shared information base. We present EVAC-AI, a knowledge-graph-grounded conversational Q\&A system designed to support all three capabilities for coastal flood evacuation planning in Virginia Beach. EVAC-AI integrates independently maintained data sources including FEMA flood zones, NOAA tide readings, evacuation routes, and Waze crowdsourced reports, into a single Neo4j knowledge graph. This graph is exposed through a natural-language query pipeline that translates user questions directly into validated, schema-refined Cypher queries, rather than retrieving subgraphs for an LLM to summarize. We argue that this design directly supports the three requirements: direct query execution preserves the structure and relationships of the graph through to the final answer, grounds multi-hop decisions in explicit and auditable graph traversals rather than generated summaries, and ensures that users in different roles receive responses backed by the same verifiable graph results. A single-page chatbot-and-map interface demonstrates the architecture in practice by returning both natural-language answers and corresponding map highlights for queries spanning flood zones, evacuation routes, and shelters.

frontier.title: Engagement-Aware Agentic Pursuit-Evasion
frontier.abstract: This paper presents a hierarchical multi-agent architecture in which independent large language model (LLM) planners perform strategic role assignment for attacking and defend- ing robot teams, decoupled from low-level control execution. At each planning cycle, each team’s LLM planner observes its own team in full but the opposing team only within its robots’ combined field of view, then assigns each robot a tactical role – e.g., hold a perimeter, neutralize an intruder on contact, or converge with teammates for capture – to- gether with a natural-language justification. Each robot in- dependently executes its assigned role through a receding- horizon model predictive control (MPC) controller, followed by a discrete-time control barrier function (CBF) filter for safety and role-dependent engagement constraints. Differen- tiated capture and neutralization incentives require the de- fending planner to balance threat resolution against resource allocation under partial observability. We evaluate the frame- work across variable-sized adversary teams using both state- based tactical reasoning and image-based contact classifi- cation. Results show that collective team behavior can be adapted through high-level LLM role assignment while re- taining the same underlying low-level control architecture.

frontier.title: Meta-Cognizing Seed AI
frontier.abstract: The Common Model of Cognition (CMC) suggests a unified view of metacognition: cognition becomes metacognitive when bounded information about the agent’s own processing enters the ordinary cognitive cycle. Here we extend that commitment from human-like impasses, episodic reconstruction, and hypothetical states to a less human-like neural-symbolic seed AI that metacognizes as it evaluates and implements proposed self-modifications. Our concrete setting is the Omega architecture: an agentic cognitive cycle combining LLMs with Hyperon symbolic memory and reasoning, in which proposals are separated from the authority to act on them, and a slower GOLEM-Iter loop rewrites the cycle’s own components under protected evaluation. Current Omega instances are LLM-heavy but designed for progressively plural neural-symbolic and predictive-coding cognition. We then define metacognitive closure as an Eilenberg-Moore algebra for a resource-bounded reflection monad – in plain terms, a lawful interface through which a system writes bounded descriptions of its own processing and demonstrably consumes them – and summarize our companion mathematical paper, The Geometry and Economics of Metacognitive Self-modification, which makes the concept quantitative: hidden probes priced by description length certify how far a self-modification departs from closure, a measured repair contraction keeps accumulated drift inside an explicit tube, and the rate of trustworthy self-modification is limited by proposal entropy and evaluation capacity. Closure is thereby the migration-coherence coordinate of a larger metacognitive competence vector, not a guarantee that the self-model, evaluator, or goals are correct. We close with an evaluation ecology tied to the formal quantities and the conditions under which the program would be falsified. The result is a research program toward AGI and potentially superintelligence, tied closely to current empirical work on Omega agents.

frontier.title: SARP: A Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning Framework for Mobile Robot Obstacle Avoidance and Path Optimization
frontier.abstract: Abstract This paper presents SARP, a Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning framework for mobile robot navigation in complex and dynamic environments. By integrating semantic embeddings from a pre-trained language encoder with reinforcement learning, SARP constructs semantically enriched state representations that combine geometric perception and contextual knowledge. A semantic-guided policy optimization mechanism aligns efficiency, safety, and task intent, while asynchronous semantic updates decouple language encoding from the high-frequency control loop. Experiments in dynamic maze, corridor crossing, and crowded field scenarios show that SARP substantially outperforms conventional reinforcement learning baselines and achieves competitive or slightly superior navigation performance compared with representative large-language-model-aware approaches, while requiring substantially lower online semantic inference overhead. Profiling on desktop and embedded NVIDIA platforms further demonstrates a favorable performance–latency trade-off for edge deployment.

frontier.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
frontier.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

CSG-Nav: Confidence-Aware Semantic-Geometric Fusion for Robust Exploration and Accurate Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation
frontier.abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation requires autonomous agents to explore unseen environments and locate target objects without task-specific training, posing challenges in perceptual reliability under observation uncertainty and physically grounded goal termination. Although foundation-model-based approaches improve generalization, they remain vulnerable to unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-induced directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect stopping decisions. To address these limitations, we propose CSG-Nav, a zero-shot navigation framework centered on confidence-aware multimodal information fusion. CSG-Nav integrates three complementary fusion mechanisms. First, semantic-source fusion integrates open-vocabulary detection results, detection confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning to produce more reliable direction-level semantic scores and suppress hallucination-induced directional bias. Second, spatial-confidence fusion weights multi-view semantic evidence using a Gaussian decay function, suppressing unreliable distant observations while accumulating spatially consistent exploration preferences. Third, semantic-geometric decision fusion combines semantic target detection with depth-based 3D localization to support physically grounded stopping decisions. Experiments on HM3Dv1, HM3Dv2, and MP3D demonstrate competitive zero-shot performance, achieving success rates of 58.9%, 71.6%, and 44.3%. Fusion-level ablations and real-world deployments in indoor and outdoor environments further verify the effectiveness and practicality of CSG-Nav for robust navigation under uncertain perception. Code is available at https://xr-ui.github.io/CSGNav.github.io/

frontier.title: RAIL: Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning for Student-Compatible Teacher Policies
frontier.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from raw sensory inputs such as images or onboard sensors can be challenging due to high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. A common strategy is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged state information and then distill it into a student policy that acts from raw inputs alone. However, when the teacher relies on information unavailable to the student, exact imitation may be impossible, creating an irreducible imitation gap. Existing approaches typically mitigate this mismatch through careful reward shaping or additional reinforcement learning on the student policy after the teacher has been trained. Instead, we introduce Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning (RAIL), which addresses the mismatch during teacher training itself. RAIL learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations using contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in this space. Because the teacher policy is constrained to operate on this shared space, it learns behaviors that are reproducible from student observations. This substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance. Across multiple environments, RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct reinforcement learning from raw observations. The learned representations further enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. Project site: https://merajmammadov.com/rail/.

frontier.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
frontier.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.

frontier.title: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
frontier.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.

Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
frontier.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

frontier.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
frontier.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

Learning contact-rich whole-body manipulation with example-guided reinforcement learning
frontier.abstract: Humans use diverse skills and strategies to effectively manipulate various objects, ranging from dexterous in-hand manipulation (fine motor skills) to complex whole-body manipulation (gross motor skills). The latter involves full-body engagement and extensive contact with various body parts beyond just the hands, where the compliance of our skin and muscles plays a crucial role in increasing contact stability and mitigating uncertainty. For robots, synthesizing these contact-rich behaviors has fundamental challenges because of the rapidly growing combinatorics inherent to this amount of contact, making explicit reasoning about all contact interactions intractable. We explore the use of example-guided reinforcement learning to generate robust whole-body skills for the manipulation of large and unwieldy objects. Our method’s effectiveness is demonstrated on Toyota Research Institute’s Punyo robot, a humanoid upper body with highly deformable, pressure-sensing skin. Training was conducted in simulation with only a single example motion per object manipulation task, and policies were easily transferred to hardware owing to domain randomization and the robot’s compliance. The resulting agent can manipulate various everyday objects, such as a water jug and large boxes, in a similar fashion to the example motion. In addition, we show blind dexterous whole-body manipulation, relying solely on proprioceptive and tactile feedback without object pose tracking. Our analysis highlights the critical role of compliance in facilitating whole-body manipulation with humanoid robots.

frontier.title: Vision–Language–Action Models for Robotic Manipulation: A Critical Review of Design Choices, Evidence, and Emerging Frontiers
frontier.abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models aim to unify perception, language grounding, and robot control, yet recent progress in robotic manipulation remains difficult to compare because systems differ widely in observation modalities, action interfaces, execution regimes, control horizons, and measurement boundaries. The counted analytical corpus comprises 59 unique works: 20 VLA systems in the settings-tuple audit, eight benchmark or evaluation-protocol studies, and 31 additional mechanism or context studies. Survey seeds and general background references are not included in this count. We organize the field through a five-axis design-space taxonomy: (A) perception encoding and spatial grounding; (B) action generation, control regime, and reasoning–control interface; (C) training and adaptation; (D) data provenance and embodiment; and (E) temporal horizon and stabilization. Across these axes, we synthesize five recurring reported limitation patterns—visual brittleness, action degeneration, static supervised fine-tuning limitation, embodiment gaps, and long-horizon breakdown—and consolidate them into four research gaps: reasoning–action decoupling, closed-loop control under contact, spatiotemporal grounding, and data/embodiment mismatch. To support auditable cross-paper interpretation, we introduce a comparability-first reporting schema, a taxonomy coding manual, canonical pseudocode for core VLA mechanisms, and an evidence-tier policy for calibrating claims. We further critique what LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and CALVIN can and cannot establish, showing that current benchmarks remain insufficient for strong deployment-level claims about contact-rich recovery, viewpoint robustness, embodiment transfer, long-horizon stability, and end-to-end latency.

frontier.title: From Rules to Autonomous Agents: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Human-AI Integration, and the Governance of Agentic Systems-A Review
frontier.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.
frontier.venue: Journal of Engineering and Applied Sciences Technology

frontier.title: Imagining Trajectories for Anomaly Detection in Reinforcement Learning from Images
frontier.abstract: Abstract Detecting anomalous inputs is a critical prerequisite for the safe deployment of reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world environments. Although anomaly detection (AD) has been extensively studied in other domains, its application to reinforcement learning remains challenging due to high-dimensional sensory observations and complex temporal dependencies. Existing approaches in this setting are limited and often rely on access to internal representations of trained agents, creating an undesirable coupling between policy and safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose ITRM, a novel approach to anomaly detection in visual reinforcement learning that is fully agent-agnostic and does not require access to policy internals. Our method is based on the observation that deviations from nominal environment dynamics can be identified through discrepancies in the latent representations of a learned world model. Specifically, we leverage predictive components of a recurrent state-space model to generate deterministic latent embeddings that serve as normative references for anomaly detection. Anomalies are detected by comparing predicted latent features against a reference set of nominal embeddings using a similarity-based criterion. Operating in the world model’s latent space allows the detector to capture semantically meaningful deviations. Extensive empirical evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong detection performance. On the Anomaly-Gym benchmark, our method outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average AUROC of 0.853 and an FPR95 of 0.279.

frontier.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
frontier.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

frontier.title: A semantic-enhanced multi-modal remote sensing foundation model for Earth observation
Generative AI and Large Language Models: Transformers, Prompt Engineering, and AI Agents
frontier.abstract: Generative AI has transitioned from the lab to the classroom, hospitals, software teams, and boardrooms. Large language models (LLMs), transformer-based foundation models, are at the heart of this paradigm change, with their ability to write texts, reason, summarize, translate, and code. However, these developments have left many students and researchers, as well as practitioners, with disjointed bits of knowledge. This book was developed with that knowledge in mind in order to streamline all that information in a single comprehensive and hands-on natural language processing (NLP) and generative AI guide. The book follows the path of the technology itself. Chapter 1 covers transformer architectures ranging from the self-attention mechanism to encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures. The course also includes lectures on mixture of experts, scaling laws, pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment and multimodal models. Targeting prompt engineering and in-context learning is the focus of Chapter 2. It uses zero shot, few shot, chain of thought prompting, system prompts and context engineering as skills to learn and test. Chapter 3 focuses on LLM reasoning and test-time compute, presenting various ways in which deep learning systems can be extended to form reasoning models, self-consistency, and search over reasoning paths. As it is not possible to know everything, Chapters 4 and 5 discuss retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). They start with embeddings and vector databases, chunking strategies and semantic search. They then transition to advanced RAG – hybrid search, reranking, knowledge graphs, GraphRAG, and agentic RAG, all while also focusing on evaluation and LLMOps for production. The strands are woven together in Chapter 6 under the umbrella of agentic AI and AI agents. It examines the use of tools, the calling of functions, the memory of an agent, as well as planning and multi-agent systems and the way autonomous agents are transforming work. Chapter 7 ends with trustworthy and responsible AI. It speaks about hallucination, bias/fairness, explainability, data privacy, AI safety, AI ethics and AI governance, as without trust, the capability cannot be sustained. The chapters are designed with learning and reference in mind for each. It introduces the foundations and outlines the key techniques side-by-side in summary tables, covers present open challenges and future directions, and concludes with practical advice. Benchmarking and evaluation is handled very transparently with regard to the deficiencies in existing approaches – and I do hope readers will take the shortcomings as a challenge and a starting point for their own work. The working levels that the book is aimed at are graduate and undergraduate students, academic researchers, machine learning engineers, data scientists, and technology leaders. Can also be used as a textbook in the course where it was used or as a builder's handbook or as a literature map for those preparing an indexed study in a Scopus journal. I'm focusing more on enduring principles than fleeting tools because no one can stay current in a science that is evolving monthly. We hope this book empowers you to grasp generative AI, create responsibly, and shape the future of AI together.

frontier.title: A Reference Architecture for Integrating Agentic AI into Enterprise Software: Responsibilities, Interactions, and Variability
frontier.abstract: Agentic AI moves generative AI applications toward systems that coordinate reasoning, enterprise context, model inference, and external actions. Integrating these capabilities into enterprise software introduces diverse architectural concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation. Existing research and industry architectures address many of these concerns but differ in scope, abstraction, responsibility organization, interaction representation, and assumptions about which capabilities are required. This paper presents a technology-neutral reference architecture for enterprise agentic AI integration. We synthesize architectural capabilities from research publications, industry architecture guidance, and interoperability specifications by architectural purpose, organize them into ten responsibilities, and define boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that distinguish responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. We instantiate the architecture as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG metric computation and reporting system, and complement the case with a mapping of an independently published agentic architecture. The case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities; different questions take different interaction paths, controls activate only under their conditions, and the probed boundary invariants hold. The independent architecture maps onto the proposed responsibilities without requiring an additional one. These results provide initial evidence for the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness. The deployment and recorded results are available as a replication package.

frontier.title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
frontier.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.

frontier.title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
frontier.abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

frontier.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
frontier.abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

frontier.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
frontier.abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $α$-divergence family.

frontier.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
frontier.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

frontier.title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
frontier.abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.

frontier.title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
frontier.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.

frontier.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
frontier.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant.
